name: Frontal bone
etymology: From Latin frons, frontis ‘forehead, front’. So it means ‘the forehead bone’ — it forms the forehead and the roofs of the orbits.
tip: Two halves fuse in early childhood; a persistent midline metopic suture is a normal variant.

name: Parietal bone
etymology: From Latin paries, parietis ‘wall’ (of a house). So it means ‘the wall bone’ — the paired bones form the side walls and roof of the cranium.
tip: Temporalis takes origin from the temporal fossa below the temporal lines on this bone.

name: Occipital bone
etymology: From Latin occiput ‘back of the head’, from ob ‘against, behind’ + caput ‘head’. So it means ‘the bone at the back of the head’.
tip: Upper trapezius, semispinalis capitis and the suboccipitals attach around the nuchal lines — the ‘yes’ nod happens at its condyles on C1.

name: Temporal bone
etymology: From Latin tempus, temporis ‘time’, via tempora ‘the temples’. Probably because the temples are where grey hair first shows the passage of time (the exact origin is uncertain). So it means ‘the bone of the temple’.
landmarks: Petrous part (houses middle and inner ear)
tip: The mastoid process is the insertion of sternocleidomastoid — palpate it just behind the earlobe.

name: Sphenoid bone
etymology: From Greek sphēn ‘wedge’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — it is wedged into the middle of the skull base between the other cranial bones.
tip: Butterfly-shaped keystone of the skull base; the lateral pterygoid plate anchors the pterygoid chewing muscles.

name: Ethmoid bone
etymology: From Greek ēthmos ‘sieve’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘sieve-like bone’ — its cribriform plate is perforated like a sieve for the olfactory nerve fibres.
tip: A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell and CSF leaking from the nose.

name: Maxilla
etymology: Latin maxilla ‘jaw, jawbone’, a diminutive related to mala ‘cheek, jaw’. So it means ‘the (upper) jaw bone’.
tip: Holds the upper teeth and the largest paranasal sinus; it is fixed — all chewing motion comes from the mandible.

name: Nasal bone
etymology: From Latin nasus ‘nose’. So it means ‘the nose bone’ — the paired bones form the bony bridge of the nose.
landmarks: Lower border attaching the lateral nasal cartilages
tip: The most commonly fractured facial bone — a ‘broken nose’ is usually these.

name: Lacrimal bone
etymology: From Latin lacrima ‘tear’. So it means ‘the tear bone’ — it holds the lacrimal (tear) sac in the inner wall of the orbit.
tip: The smallest and most fragile facial bone, in the medial wall of the orbit.

name: Zygomatic bone
etymology: From Greek zygōma ‘bar, bolt’, from zygon ‘yoke’. So it means ‘the yoke bone’ — it yokes the face to the side of the skull via the zygomatic arch.
tip: The cheekbone; masseter arises from the zygomatic arch.

name: Palatine bone
etymology: From Latin palatum ‘palate, roof of the mouth’. So it means ‘the palate bone’ — its horizontal plate forms the back of the hard palate.
tip: Forms the posterior third of the hard palate; the soft palate hangs from its back edge.

name: Vomer
etymology: Latin vomer ‘ploughshare’. So it means ‘the ploughshare bone’ — a thin blade shaped like a plough blade.
landmarks: Posteroinferior part of the nasal septum
tip: With the ethmoid’s perpendicular plate it forms the bony nasal septum — a deviated septum often involves it.

name: Inferior nasal concha
etymology: From Latin concha ‘shell’ (Greek konchē ‘mussel, shell’). So it means ‘the lower shell of the nose’ — a curled, shell-like scroll of bone on the lateral nasal wall.
landmarks: Overhangs the inferior meatus (opening of the nasolacrimal duct)
tip: Unlike the superior and middle conchae (parts of the ethmoid) it is a separate bone.

name: Mandible
etymology: From Latin mandibula ‘jaw’, from mandere ‘to chew’. So it means ‘the chewing bone’ — the movable lower jaw.
tip: The only freely movable skull bone (besides the ossicles); temporalis inserts on the coronoid process, masseter on the ramus and angle.

name: Hyoid bone
etymology: From Greek hyoeidēs ‘shaped like the letter upsilon (υ)’. So it means ‘U-shaped bone’ — exactly its shape in the front of the neck.
articulations: No bony articulation — suspended by muscles and the stylohyoid ligaments
tip: Sits at about C3; anchor for the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles that move it during swallowing.

name: Malleus
etymology: Latin malleus ‘hammer, mallet’. So it means ‘the hammer’ — its handle and head look like a small hammer.
tip: Tensor tympani inserts on its handle to damp loud sounds.

name: Incus
etymology: Latin incus ‘anvil’. So it means ‘the anvil’ — the hammer (malleus) appears to strike it.
tip: The middle of the three ossicles, passing vibration from malleus to stapes.

name: Stapes
etymology: Medieval Latin stapes ‘stirrup’. So it means ‘the stirrup’ — two crura and a footplate look exactly like a stirrup.
articulations: Oval window (footplate held by annular ligament)
tip: The smallest bone in the body; stapedius (the smallest muscle) attaches to its neck.

name: Atlas (C1)
etymology: Named after Atlas, the Greek Titan who held up the heavens on his shoulders. So it means ‘the bone that holds up the globe of the head’.
articulations: Axis (median atlanto-axial joint with the dens, and lateral atlanto-axial joints — rotation ‘no’)
tip: A ring of bone with no body; its large transverse process can be felt between the mastoid process and the angle of the mandible.

name: Axis (C2)
etymology: From Latin axis ‘axle, pivot’. So it means ‘the pivot’ — the atlas and head rotate around its dens like a wheel on an axle.
tip: About half of all neck rotation happens at C1–C2; its large spinous process is the first bony bump felt below the occiput.

name: C3 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the third neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C2 and C4
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
tip: C3 sits behind the hyoid bone — the first typical cervical vertebra below the specialised C1–C2 pair.

name: C4 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the fourth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C3 and C5
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
Level of the upper thyroid cartilage / carotid bifurcation
tip: C4 lies roughly at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, where the common carotid artery usually bifurcates; the C4 root helps form the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).

name: C5 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the fifth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C4 and C6
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
tip: C5–C6 is the most common level for cervical disc degeneration; the C5 root (deltoid, biceps) exits above C5.

name: C6 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ is from Latin cervix ‘neck’, so this is the sixth neck vertebra.
articulations: Uncovertebral joints with C5 and C7
landmarks: Typical cervical: small oval body, triangular vertebral foramen
Anterior and posterior tubercles of the transverse process
Carotid tubercle (enlarged anterior tubercle of transverse process)
tip: C6 has the prominent carotid (Chassaignac’s) tubercle — the common carotid can be compressed against it; level of the cricoid cartilage, where larynx becomes trachea and pharynx becomes oesophagus.

name: C7 vertebra (vertebra prominens)
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Cervical’ from Latin cervix ‘neck’; prominens is Latin ‘projecting’ — named for its long, easily felt spinous process.
landmarks: Long, non-bifid spinous process (ends in a tubercle)
Small transverse foramina (vertebral artery usually enters at C6, not C7)
tip: The most prominent spinous process at the base of the neck — the usual starting point for counting vertebrae (T1 can be equally prominent; C7 slides forward under your finger on neck flexion-extension).

name: T1 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the first chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 1.
articulations: Rib 1 head (full facet) and rib 2 head (demifacet)
landmarks: Full (whole) superior costal facet for the head of rib 1
Cervical-like body with small uncinate lips
tip: T1’s spinous process is often as prominent as C7’s; its full facet for rib 1 makes it unique among the upper thoracic vertebrae.

name: T2 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the second chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 2.
tip: The jugular (suprasternal) notch lies at about the T2–T3 level.

name: T3 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the third chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 3.
tip: The T3 spinous process is level with the root of the spine of the scapula (arms by the sides).

name: T4 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the fourth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 4.
tip: The sternal angle lines up with the T4–T5 disc — the plane of the tracheal bifurcation and the start and end of the aortic arch.

name: T5 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the fifth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 5.
landmarks: Body may be flattened on the left by the descending aorta
tip: Typical mid-thoracic vertebra: steep, overlapping spinous processes limit extension in this region.

name: T6 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the sixth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 6.
landmarks: Heart-shaped body, long downward-sloping spinous process
tip: The textbook ‘typical’ thoracic vertebra — its spinous tip lies over the body of the vertebra below.

name: T7 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the seventh chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 7.
tip: The inferior angle of the scapula sits level with the T7 spinous process (arms by the sides) — a handy counting landmark.

name: T8 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the eighth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 8.
tip: The inferior vena cava passes through the diaphragm at about the T8 level.

name: T9 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the ninth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 9.
landmarks: Inferior demifacet for rib 10 often small or absent
tip: The xiphisternal joint lies at about the T9 level.

name: T10 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the tenth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 10.
articulations: Tubercle of rib 10 (costotransverse joint, when present)
landmarks: Usually a single whole costal facet for rib 10 (body/pedicle junction)
Transverse costal facet small or absent
tip: The oesophagus passes through the diaphragm at about the T10 level.

name: T11 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the eleventh chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 11.
landmarks: Single whole costal facet for rib 11 on the pedicle
No transverse costal facet (rib 11 has no tubercle articulation)
tip: A transitional vertebra: no transverse-process rib joint, so rotation starts to be restricted.

name: T12 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Thoracic’ is from Greek thōrax ‘breastplate, chest’, so this is the twelfth chest vertebra — the one that carries rib 12.
landmarks: Single whole costal facet for rib 12
Thoracic-type superior and lumbar-type inferior articular processes
tip: The thoracolumbar junction — a common site of osteoporotic compression fractures; the aorta passes through the diaphragm at T12.

name: L1 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the first vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Kidney-shaped body, no costal facets or transverse foramina
tip: In adults the spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at L1–L2; the transpyloric plane crosses L1.

name: L2 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the second vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Attachment of the diaphragmatic crura (right L1–L3, left L1–L2)
tip: Psoas major arises from the bodies and transverse processes of T12–L4/L5, including L2; L2 is in the middle of its origin.

name: L3 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the third vertebra of the loin (low back).
tip: Sits at the apex of the lumbar lordosis; its long transverse processes are a big lever for quadratus lumborum and the thoracolumbar fascia.

name: L4 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the fourth vertebra of the loin (low back).
landmarks: Spinous process level with the tops of the iliac crests (supracristal plane, L4 or L4–L5)
tip: Draw a line between the iliac crest tops to find L4 — the usual landmark for lumbar puncture at L3–L4 or L4–L5; the aorta bifurcates at L4.

name: L5 vertebra
etymology: From Latin vertebra ‘joint (of the spine)’, from vertere ‘to turn’ — the bones on which the back turns. ‘Lumbar’ is from Latin lumbus ‘loin’, so this is the fifth vertebra of the loin (low back).
articulations: Sacrum (lumbosacral joint: L5–S1 disc and facets)
Ilium (via iliolumbar ligament, not a synovial joint)
landmarks: Largest lumbar body, wedge-shaped (taller in front)
Massive transverse processes joined to the ilium by the iliolumbar ligament
tip: Its wedge shape creates the lumbosacral angle; L5 is the commonest site of spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis, and L4–L5/L5–S1 discs herniate most often.

name: Sacrum
etymology: From Latin os sacrum ‘sacred bone’, a translation of Greek hieron osteon. Why it was ‘sacred’ is uncertain — probably because it was the part offered in sacrifices, or thought to be indestructible. So it means ‘the sacred bone’ at the back of the pelvis.
articulations: Ilium of each hip bone (sacroiliac joints)
tip: The dimples of Venus mark the posterior superior iliac spines — the SI joints lie just deep to them, at about S2.

name: Coccyx
etymology: From Greek kokkyx ‘cuckoo’. So it means ‘the cuckoo bone’ — its tapering shape was likened to a cuckoo’s beak.
tip: The tailbone: gluteus maximus, coccygeus and levator ani (via the anococcygeal body) attach to it.

name: Sternum — body
etymology: Sternum from Greek sternon ‘chest, breast’. The body was historically called the gladiolus (Latin ‘small sword’, the blade of the sword-shaped sternum). So it means ‘the blade of the breastbone’.
articulations: Costal cartilages of ribs 2 (in part) to 7 (sternocostal joints)
tip: CPR compressions go on the lower half of the sternal body — above the xiphoid.

name: Sternum — manubrium
etymology: Sternum from Greek sternon ‘chest’; manubrium is Latin ‘handle’. The sternum was likened to a sword, so it means ‘the handle of the breastbone’.
articulations: Costal cartilage of rib 2 (in part, at the sternal angle)
tip: Find the sternal angle and slide sideways to locate rib 2 — the standard way to count ribs.

name: Sternum — xiphoid process
etymology: From Greek xiphos ‘sword’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘the sword-shaped process’ — the pointed tip of the sword-like sternum.
landmarks: Pointed tip, cartilaginous in youth (ossifies around age 40)
Attachment of the sternal part of the diaphragm
Attachment of rectus abdominis (anterior surface, with cartilages 5–7)
tip: Keep your hands off it in CPR — compressing the xiphoid can injure the liver.

name: 1st rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The first costa — a true rib (vertebrosternal) and atypical. True ribs reach the sternum by their own cartilage; false ribs do not; floating ribs have no front attachment.
articulations: T1 body (costovertebral joint — single facet on the head)
landmarks: Shortest, broadest and most curved rib; flat with superior and inferior surfaces
Groove for subclavian vein (in front of the tubercle)
Groove for subclavian artery and lower brachial plexus trunk (behind the tubercle)
tip: Lies largely behind the clavicle; a cervical rib or tight scalenes here can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.

name: 2nd rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The second costa — a true rib and atypical.
articulations: Sternum at the sternal angle via its costal cartilage
landmarks: About twice the length of rib 1, thinner and less curved
Tuberosity for serratus anterior on its outer surface
tip: Its cartilage meets the sternal angle — the first rib you can reliably count from the front.

name: 3rd rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The third costa — a true rib (vertebrosternal) and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
tip: Pectoralis minor arises from ribs 3–5 — a tight pec minor tilts the scapula forward.

name: 4th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The fourth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Origin of pectoralis minor (ribs 3–5) and serratus anterior slips
tip: In men the nipple usually lies over the 4th intercostal space, just below this rib.

name: 5th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The fifth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Costal cartilage receives part of rectus abdominis (cartilages 5–7)
tip: The apex beat of the heart is felt in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line — just below this rib.

name: 6th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The sixth costa — a true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum via its costal cartilage (sternocostal joint)
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage gives origin to the sternocostal head of pectoralis major (cartilages 1–6) and part of rectus abdominis
tip: Intercostal nerves run in the costal groove under each rib — needles go just above a rib, never below.

name: 7th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The seventh costa — the last true rib and typical.
articulations: Sternum near the xiphisternal junction via its costal cartilage
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage gives insertion to rectus abdominis
tip: The last rib whose own cartilage reaches the sternum (ribs 1–7 are ‘true’ ribs).

name: 8th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The eighth costa — the first false rib (vertebrochondral) and typical.
landmarks: Typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage forms part of the costal margin
tip: Its cartilage joins the one above rather than the sternum — the first ‘false’ rib; cartilages 7–10 form the costal margin.

name: 9th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The ninth costa — a false rib (vertebrochondral) and typical.
landmarks: Last typical rib: head with two facets, neck, tubercle, angle, costal groove
Cartilage forms part of the costal margin
tip: Lower-rib fractures (8–12) on the right can injure the liver, on the left the spleen.

name: 10th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The tenth costa — the last false rib and atypical.
articulations: T10 body (costovertebral joint — usually a single facet on the head)
landmarks: Usually a single facet on the head
Tubercle, angle and costal groove present
Forms the lowest point of the costal margin
tip: The lowest point of the costal margin, at the 10th costal cartilage, marks the subcostal plane (about L3).

name: 11th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The eleventh costa — a floating rib (vertebral) and atypical.
articulations: Anterior end free in the abdominal wall muscles
landmarks: No tubercle (no articulation with the transverse process); neck indistinct
Slight angle and shallow costal groove
tip: A floating rib — its tip ends in the abdominal wall, so it has no anterior attachment.

name: 12th rib
etymology: From Latin costa ‘rib’ (hence costal, intercostal). The twelfth costa — a floating rib (vertebral) and atypical.
articulations: Anterior end free in the posterior abdominal wall
landmarks: Shortest of the lower ribs (length varies a lot)
No tubercle, no angle, no costal groove
Attachment of quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm (lateral arcuate ligament region)
tip: Quadratus lumborum pulls down on it in forced expiration; the kidney and pleura lie just in front of it.

name: Clavicle
etymology: From Latin clavicula ‘little key’, diminutive of clavis ‘key’. Probably because it rotates along its long axis like a key turning in a lock (or resembles an ancient key). So it means ‘the little key bone’.
articulations: Costal cartilage of rib 1 (via costoclavicular ligament)
tip: The most commonly fractured bone, usually at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds; the only bony link between arm and trunk.

name: Scapula
etymology: Latin scapula ‘shoulder blade’ (classically used in the plural scapulae ‘the shoulders’); probably related to a root meaning ‘to dig’, likening it to a spade. So it means ‘the shoulder blade’.
tip: Seventeen muscles attach to it — rotator cuff, deltoid, traps, rhomboids, serratus anterior, biceps, triceps long head and more.

name: Humerus
etymology: From Latin umerus ‘shoulder, upper arm’ (the h was added later). So it means ‘the shoulder/upper-arm bone’.
tip: Surgical-neck fractures endanger the axillary nerve; mid-shaft fractures the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

name: Radius
etymology: Latin radius ‘spoke of a wheel, ray’. So it means ‘the spoke’ — in pronation and supination it swings around the ulna like a spoke around a hub.
tip: Thumb-side forearm bone; a fall on an outstretched hand classically breaks its distal end (Colles fracture).

name: Ulna
etymology: Latin ulna ‘elbow, forearm’ (related to English ‘ell’, an old forearm-length measure). So it means ‘the elbow bone’ — its olecranon is the point of the elbow.
articulations: Triquetrum and lunate indirectly, via the articular disc (TFCC)
tip: Little-finger-side forearm bone; the olecranon is the point of the elbow you lean on, and the hook of the trochlear notch makes it the elbow’s main hinge.

name: Scaphoid
etymology: From Greek skaphē ‘boat, skiff’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘boat-shaped bone’ — its concave surface was likened to a small boat. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Tubercle (palpable at the wrist crease, base of thenar eminence)
tip: The most commonly fractured carpal; snuffbox tenderness after a fall needs imaging, as waist fractures risk avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.

name: Lunate
etymology: From Latin luna ‘moon’. So it means ‘moon-shaped bone’ — it is crescent-shaped. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Concave distal surface for the capitate
tip: The most commonly dislocated carpal (can compress the median nerve); avascular necrosis of it is Kienböck’s disease.

name: Triquetrum
etymology: From Latin triquetrus ‘three-cornered, triangular’. So it means ‘the triangular bone’ — pyramid-shaped. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Oval facet for the pisiform on its palmar surface
tip: The second most commonly fractured carpal — typically a dorsal chip from a fall onto the back of the hand.

name: Pisiform
etymology: From Latin pisum ‘pea’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘pea-shaped bone’ — small and round. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
tip: The bony pea you can feel at the base of the hypothenar eminence; FCU pulls through it via the pisohamate/pisometacarpal ligaments.

name: Trapezium
etymology: From Greek trapezion ‘little table’ (a four-sided figure). So it means ‘the little table bone’ — irregular and four-sided. Remember: trapeziUM is by the thUMb. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Groove for the flexor carpi radialis tendon
tip: Its saddle joint with the 1st metacarpal gives the thumb opposition — and is a classic site of osteoarthritis.

name: Trapezoid
etymology: From Greek trapezoeidēs ‘table-shaped’ (trapeza ‘table’ + -oeidēs ‘like’). So it means ‘shaped like a little table’ — a small wedge-like four-sided bone. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
landmarks: Smallest bone of the distal row
Fits into the notched base of the 2nd metacarpal
tip: Locks into the forked base of the 2nd metacarpal, making the index ray the stable ‘fixed’ unit of the hand.

name: Capitate
etymology: From Latin caput ‘head’ (capitatus ‘having a head’). So it means ‘the bone with a head’ — its rounded head fits into the lunate and scaphoid. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
tip: The largest and most central carpal — the axis around which wrist movement is often described; aligned with the 3rd metacarpal.

name: Hamate
etymology: From Latin hamatus ‘hooked’, from hamus ‘hook’. So it means ‘the hooked bone’ — named for the hook projecting from its palmar surface. Carpal is from Greek karpos ‘wrist’.
tip: The hook can fracture from the butt of a golf club, bat or racket pressing into the palm.

name: 1st metacarpal (thumb)
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm. This one supports the thumb.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the thumb (MCP joint)
landmarks: Insertion of opponens pollicis (shaft) and abductor pollicis longus (base)
Two sesamoids at the palmar head
tip: A fracture-dislocation of its base is a Bennett’s fracture; it lies in a different plane, letting the thumb oppose.

name: 2nd metacarpal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the index finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Insertion of extensor carpi radialis longus (dorsal base) and flexor carpi radialis (palmar base)
tip: Its keyed-in base makes the index CMC joint almost immobile — the stable post of the hand.

name: 3rd metacarpal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Styloid process on the dorsal base
Insertion of extensor carpi radialis brevis (base)
Origin of adductor pollicis (transverse head, shaft)
tip: The only metacarpal with a styloid process, where ECRB inserts; with the 2nd it forms the rigid central column.

name: 4th metacarpal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Small quadrilateral base with facets for capitate and hamate
tip: Its CMC joint is mobile, letting the ulnar side of the palm cup for grip.

name: 5th metacarpal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + karpos ‘wrist’. So metacarpal means ‘the bone beyond the wrist’ — the bones of the palm.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the little finger (MCP joint)
landmarks: Tubercle on the medial base (extensor carpi ulnaris)
tip: A punch with a closed fist commonly breaks its neck — the ‘boxer’s fracture’.

name: Proximal phalanx of the thumb
parts: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the palm. The thumb is pollex in Latin (hence ‘pollicis’ in muscle names). The thumb has only two phalanges (no middle one).
articulations: Distal phalanx of the thumb (IP joint)
landmarks: Abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis (radial base, via the radial sesamoid)
Adductor pollicis (ulnar base, via the ulnar sesamoid)
tip: Skier’s/gamekeeper’s thumb is a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament at the MCP joint on its base.

name: Proximal phalanx of the index finger
parts: Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the palm. Index is Latin ‘pointer’, from indicare ‘to point out’.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the index finger (PIP joint)
landmarks: 1st dorsal interosseous (radial side of base/extensor expansion)
tip: The 1st dorsal interosseous abducts the index on this bone — the muscle bulk in the first web space.

name: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger
parts: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the palm. The middle finger is digitus medius in Latin.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the middle finger (PIP joint)
tip: The middle finger is the axis for finger abduction/adduction, so only dorsal interossei attach to it — one on each side.

name: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger
parts: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the palm. The ring finger is digitus anularis in Latin (anulus ‘ring’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the ring finger (PIP joint)
tip: Palmar interossei adduct toward the middle finger, dorsal ones abduct away — here they pull on opposite sides of the base.

name: Proximal phalanx of the little finger
parts: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the palm. The little finger is digitus minimus in Latin (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the little finger (PIP joint)
landmarks: Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis (ulnar side of base)
tip: The hypothenar muscles insert on its base, so it moves with the little-finger side of the palm.

name: Middle phalanx of the index finger
parts: Middle phalanx of second finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three. Index is Latin ‘pointer’, from indicare ‘to point out’.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the index finger (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the index finger (DIP joint)
landmarks: Base with two concave facets and a median ridge
Flexor digitorum superficialis splits to insert on both sides of the shaft
Central slip of the extensor expansion (dorsal base)
tip: Test index FDS by holding the other fingers straight and asking for PIP flexion.

name: Middle phalanx of the middle finger
parts: Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three. The middle finger is digitus medius in Latin.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the middle finger (DIP joint)
landmarks: Base with two concave facets and a median ridge
FDS insertion on both sides of the shaft
Central slip of extensor expansion (dorsal base)
tip: The middle finger is the longest digit, and its middle phalanx is usually the longest one in the hand.

name: Middle phalanx of the ring finger
parts: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three. The ring finger is digitus anularis in Latin (anulus ‘ring’).
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the ring finger (DIP joint)
landmarks: Base with two concave facets and a median ridge
FDS insertion on both sides of the shaft
Central slip of extensor expansion (dorsal base)
tip: Rupture of the central slip at its base gives a boutonnière deformity (PIP flexed, DIP hyperextended).

name: Middle phalanx of the little finger
parts: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three. The little finger is digitus minimus in Latin (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the little finger (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the little finger (DIP joint)
landmarks: Base with two concave facets and a median ridge
Shortest middle phalanx of the hand
FDS insertion (tendon sometimes small or absent)
Central slip of extensor expansion (dorsal base)
tip: Little-finger FDS is weak or absent in some people, so PIP flexion may rely on FDP.

name: Distal phalanx of the thumb
parts: Distal phalanx of first finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest from the palm — the fingertip bone. The thumb is pollex in Latin (hence ‘pollicis’ in muscle names). The thumb has only two phalanges (no middle one).
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the thumb (IP joint)
tip: FPL is the only muscle that flexes the thumb IP joint — bending the thumb tip tests it (anterior interosseous nerve).

name: Distal phalanx of the index finger
parts: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest from the palm — the fingertip bone. Index is Latin ‘pointer’, from indicare ‘to point out’.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the index finger (DIP joint)
tip: Mallet finger: the terminal extensor tendon pulls off its dorsal base and the DIP droops.

name: Distal phalanx of the middle finger
parts: Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest from the palm — the fingertip bone. The middle finger is digitus medius in Latin.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the middle finger (DIP joint)
tip: Only FDP flexes the DIP joint — hold the middle phalanx still and bend the tip to test it.

name: Distal phalanx of the ring finger
parts: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest from the palm — the fingertip bone. The ring finger is digitus anularis in Latin (anulus ‘ring’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the ring finger (DIP joint)
tip: Jersey finger — FDP avulsion from its base when grabbing a shirt — most often involves the ring finger.

name: Distal phalanx of the little finger
parts: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the finger bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest from the palm — the fingertip bone. The little finger is digitus minimus in Latin (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the little finger (DIP joint)
tip: FDP to the ring and little fingers is supplied by the ulnar nerve — weak tip flexion here suggests ulnar nerve damage.

name: Hip bone (os coxae)
etymology: Os coxae is Latin ‘bone of the hip’ (coxa ‘hip’). It fuses from three bones: ilium, from Latin ilia ‘flanks, loins’; ischium, from Greek ischion ‘hip joint, haunch’; and pubis, from Latin (os) pubis, from pubes ‘grown-up, adult’ — named for the hair that appears over it at puberty. So: the flank part, the sitting/haunch part and the ‘adult’ part.
landmarks: Ilium: iliac crest, ASIS, AIIS, PSIS, PSIS dimples, iliac fossa, gluteal lines, auricular surface
Ischium: ischial tuberosity (sit bone), ischial spine, ischial ramus
Pubis: pubic tubercle, pubic crest, symphyseal surface, superior and inferior pubic rami
Acetabulum (all three bones meet here at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage)
tip: The ischial tuberosity is the hamstrings’ origin; the ASIS is the origin of sartorius and the standard landmark for pelvic tilt.

name: Femur
etymology: Latin femur ‘thigh’. So it simply means ‘the thigh bone’.
tip: The longest and strongest bone; neck fractures in older adults can cut off the blood supply to the head.

name: Patella
etymology: Latin patella ‘small dish, small pan’, diminutive of patina ‘dish’. So it means ‘the little dish’ — a flat, rounded plate at the front of the knee.
landmarks: Lateral and medial articular facets (lateral larger)
tip: The largest sesamoid bone, in the quadriceps tendon; it lengthens the quads’ lever arm for knee extension.

name: Tibia
etymology: Latin tibia ‘shin bone’, also ‘flute, pipe’ — probably because early flutes were made from animal shin bones. So it means ‘the shin bone’.
tip: Its anterior border lies just under the skin — the ‘shin’ — which is why shin fractures are often open.

name: Fibula
etymology: Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’. Probably because the slender fibula beside the tibia looks like the pin of a brooch. So it means ‘the pin bone’.
articulations: Talus (lateral malleolus, part of the ankle joint)
tip: Biceps femoris and the LCL attach to its head; the common fibular nerve wraps around its neck, where it is easily injured.

name: Talus
etymology: Latin talus ‘ankle bone, knucklebone’ — ankle bones of animals were used as dice. So it means ‘the ankle bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Posterior process with medial and lateral tubercles
tip: No muscles attach to it; its trochlea is wider in front, so the ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion.

name: Calcaneus
etymology: From Latin calx, calcis ‘heel’ (also ‘lime, chalk’). So it means ‘the heel bone’.
landmarks: Medial and lateral processes of the tuberosity (plantar fascia)
tip: The largest tarsal; the Achilles tendon inserts on its tuberosity and plantar fasciitis pain sits at its medial process.

name: Navicular
etymology: From Latin navicula ‘little boat’, diminutive of navis ‘ship’. So it means ‘boat-shaped bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Concave proximal surface for the talar head
Three facets distally for the cuneiforms
tip: Its tuberosity is palpable in front of the medial malleolus — the landmark for the navicular drop test of arch collapse.

name: Cuboid
etymology: From Greek kybos ‘cube’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘cube-shaped bone’. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Groove for the fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon
tip: Fibularis longus runs in its plantar groove on the way to the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform.

name: Medial cuneiform
etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Insertion of tibialis anterior and fibularis longus (with base of 1st metatarsal)
Lisfranc ligament attachment (to the 2nd metatarsal base)
tip: Tibialis anterior and fibularis longus insert side by side on it, acting like a stirrup under the medial arch.

name: Intermediate cuneiform
etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Set back (recessed) so the 2nd metatarsal base keys in between the medial and lateral cuneiforms
tip: Its recessed position locks the 2nd metatarsal base — the keystone of the Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) joint.

name: Lateral cuneiform
etymology: From Latin cuneus ‘wedge’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘wedge-shaped bone’ — the three cuneiforms form the transverse arch like wedges in a Roman arch. Tarsal is from Greek tarsos ‘flat surface, wicker frame’ (originally the sole/flat of the foot).
landmarks: Origin of part of flexor hallucis brevis
tip: Sits between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, linking the medial and lateral columns of the foot.

name: 1st metatarsal (big toe)
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the big toe (MTP joint)
Medial and lateral sesamoids (under the head)
landmarks: Tuberosity on the plantar base (fibularis longus)
Grooves under the head for the two sesamoids
tip: Takes the most load at push-off; hallux valgus (bunion) angles its head medially.

name: 2nd metatarsal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 2nd toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Base recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms
Lisfranc ligament attachment (from the medial cuneiform)
tip: Its rigid, keyed-in base makes it the classic site of a metatarsal stress (‘march’) fracture.

name: 3rd metatarsal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 3rd toe (MTP joint)
tip: Also a common stress-fracture site; with the 2nd it forms the stiff central forefoot.

name: 4th metatarsal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 4th toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Quadrilateral base articulating with the cuboid
tip: Part of the mobile lateral column — its joint with the cuboid lets the outer forefoot adapt to the ground.

name: 5th metatarsal
etymology: From Greek meta ‘beyond, after’ + tarsos ‘flat of the foot’. So metatarsal means ‘the bone beyond the tarsus’ — the long bones of the forefoot.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 5th toe (MTP joint)
landmarks: Tuberosity on the lateral base (fibularis brevis)
Origin of flexor digiti minimi brevis
tip: An inversion sprain can avulse its tuberosity; a Jones fracture is just beyond, at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, and heals poorly.

name: Proximal phalanx of the big toe
parts: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the sole. The big toe is the hallux in Latin (hence ‘hallucis’ in muscle names); it has only two phalanges (no middle one).
articulations: Distal phalanx of the big toe (IP joint)
landmarks: Flexor hallucis brevis (both sides of base, via the sesamoids)
tip: Hallux valgus drifts it laterally on the 1st metatarsal head; ‘turf toe’ is a plantar-plate sprain at its base.

name: Proximal phalanx of the 2nd toe
parts: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the sole.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 2nd toe (PIP joint)
tip: The 2nd toe is the foot’s axis, so only dorsal interossei attach to it; hammer toe most often involves this toe.

name: Proximal phalanx of the 3rd toe
parts: Proximal phalanx of third finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the sole.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 3rd toe (PIP joint)
tip: Plantar interossei adduct toes 3–5 toward the 2nd toe; dorsal interossei abduct away from it.

name: Proximal phalanx of the 4th toe
parts: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the sole.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 4th toe (PIP joint)
tip: Lesser-toe proximal phalanges are long and slender compared with the stubby middle and distal ones.

name: Proximal phalanx of the 5th toe
aka: Proximal phalanx of the little toe
parts: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Proximal (Latin proximus ‘nearest’) means the one nearest the sole. The little toe is digitus minimus (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 5th toe (PIP joint)
landmarks: Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis (lateral base)
tip: A stubbed little toe most often fractures this phalanx.

name: Middle phalanx of the 2nd toe
parts: Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 2nd toe (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the 2nd toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Flexor digitorum brevis (both sides of the shaft)
tip: In a hammer toe the PIP joint between this bone and the proximal phalanx is fixed in flexion.

name: Middle phalanx of the 3rd toe
parts: Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 3rd toe (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the 3rd toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Flexor digitorum brevis (both sides of the shaft)
tip: Flexor digitorum brevis (‘short toe flexor’) inserts on the middle phalanges of toes 2–5 and flexes the PIP joints.

name: Middle phalanx of the 4th toe
parts: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 4th toe (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the 4th toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Flexor digitorum brevis (both sides of the shaft)
tip: Middle phalanges of the lesser toes are short, almost cube-like bones.

name: Middle phalanx of the 5th toe
aka: Middle phalanx of the little toe
parts: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Middle means the second of the three. The little toe is digitus minimus (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the 5th toe (PIP joint)
Distal phalanx of the 5th toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Flexor digitorum brevis slip (often small or absent)
Frequently fused with the distal phalanx (symphalangism)
tip: Often fused with the distal phalanx, so many little toes appear to have only two phalanges.

name: Distal phalanx of the big toe
parts: Distal phalanx of first finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest away — the toe-tip bone. The big toe is the hallux in Latin (hence ‘hallucis’ in muscle names); it has only two phalanges (no middle one).
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the big toe (IP joint)
tip: FHL inserts here — the last tendon to push off the ground in gait.

name: Distal phalanx of the 2nd toe
parts: Distal phalanx of second finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest away — the toe-tip bone.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 2nd toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Extensor digitorum longus/brevis via extensor expansion (dorsal base)
tip: FDL inserts on the distal phalanges of toes 2–5, curling the toes to grip the ground.

name: Distal phalanx of the 3rd toe
parts: Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest away — the toe-tip bone.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 3rd toe (DIP joint)
tip: Mallet toe is fixed flexion at the DIP joint just proximal to this bone.

name: Distal phalanx of the 4th toe
parts: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest away — the toe-tip bone.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 4th toe (DIP joint)
tip: A tiny tufted bone supporting the nail bed of the 4th toe.

name: Distal phalanx of the 5th toe
aka: Distal phalanx of the little toe
parts: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
etymology: From Greek phalanx ‘a line of soldiers in battle formation’ (plural phalanges) — the toe bones are lined up in rows like ranks of soldiers. Distal (from Latin distare ‘to stand apart’) means the one furthest away — the toe-tip bone. The little toe is digitus minimus (hence ‘digiti minimi’).
articulations: Middle phalanx of the 5th toe (DIP joint)
landmarks: Often fused with the middle phalanx
tip: The smallest phalanx in the foot; frequently fused with the middle phalanx.

name: Sesamoid bones of the foot (hallux sesamoids)
etymology: From Greek sēsamon ‘sesame seed’ + -oeidēs ‘like’. So it means ‘shaped like a sesame seed’ — small, oval bones embedded in tendons.
articulations: Plantar surface of the 1st metatarsal head (grooves)
landmarks: Within the two tendons of flexor hallucis brevis
Attachments of abductor hallucis (medial) and adductor hallucis (lateral)
tip: They take load under the big-toe ball and protect the FHL tendon; sesamoiditis is common in runners and dancers.
